title: SMOTE for Handling Imbalanced Data Problem: A Review
venue: IEEE conference (proceedings name not in PDF text)

sources: artificial (as reported for surveyed K-means SMOTE study)
datasets.notes: No own experiments. Defines IR = N_maj / N_min (Eq. 1), dataset imbalanced if IR > 1. Data sources only mentioned when summarizing surveyed studies (UCI, KEEL, artificial data for K-means SMOTE).

metric_details: Despite the abstract promising a review of 'performance evaluation in imbalanced data', the paper has no dedicated evaluation section. Sec. II only argues that overall accuracy is maximized on the majority class and fails to reflect minority-class performance, and defines the imbalance ratio IR (Eq. 1). Metrics appear only incidentally when summarizing surveyed methods: mean rank over classifiers/datasets (K-means SMOTE, with LR, KNN, GBM on UCI/KEEL/artificial data), Kappa and accuracy as fitness for PSO/BAT-tuned SMOTE, F-measure and G-mean gains for GASMOTE, TP rate and F-value for Borderline-SMOTE, accuracy and precision for Farthest SMOTE. No recommendation on protocols, statistical tests, or resampling-inside-CV.
tuning: Discusses that SMOTE parameters (k, sampling rate N) are set arbitrarily, k=5 being the common default; reviews metaheuristic (PSO, BAT, GA) tuning of k and N (Sec. IV-B).
stat_test_details: No statistical testing discussed or recommended.
reporting_details: Survey output: Table I summarizes five categories of SMOTE extensions (clustering, metaheuristic, initial selection, filtering, dimensionality changes) with advantages, limitations and references; Fig. 1 illustrates overlap, noise, small disjuncts.
key_result: Categorizes recent SMOTE extensions into clustering, metaheuristic, initial-selection, filtering and dimensionality-change families and identifies overlap, small disjuncts and small sample size as open challenges.
eval_strengths: Notes that accuracy is misleading under imbalance and that data difficulty factors (noise, overlap, small disjuncts) matter beyond IR.
eval_weaknesses: No own experiments and no substantive guidance on metrics, validation protocol or statistical testing despite the abstract claiming coverage of performance evaluation.
where: Sec. II (accuracy critique, IR Eq. 1), Sec. IV (surveyed results), Table I

title: Stop Oversampling for Class Imbalance Learning: A Critical Review

datasets.ir_range: 28.1-41.4 (Yeast4/5/6, computed from Table 2 counts; Vehicle3 IR not reported)
datasets.notes: Yeast4 (51/1433), Yeast5 (44/1440), Yeast6 (35/1449), 10 attributes each (Table 2), cited to UCI repository [189]; Vehicle3 used only as an extra check on the 8 best methods (Table 4). Multiclass deliberately excluded since most oversamplers are binary.

baselines: 72 oversamplers M1-M72 incl. SMOTE, SMOTE-TomekLinks, SMOTE-ENN, Borderline-SMOTE1/2, ADASYN, Safe-Level-SMOTE, MWMOTE, ProWSyn, SMOTE-IPF, SMOTE-RSB, CCR, G-SMOTE, DSMOTE, NRAS, SOI-CJ, ROSE, MDO
metric_details: Review side (Sec. 2, Table 1): catalogues 72 oversampling papers by #datasets (1 to 66), #classes (almost all binary, about 5 multiclass), classifiers (C4.5 most frequent, then SVM, KNN, NB, ANN) and metrics (Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F-measure, G-mean, Specificity, Kappa, MCC, AUC, TP/FP/TN/FN, ROC). Core critique: every method is validated only by downstream classification metrics on oversampled data, assuming synthetic points truly belong to the minority; such metrics can look good when models overfit synthetic data. Proposes instead a data-validity check: hide 10/25/50% of majority examples, oversample the rest, then label each synthetic point by Hassanat-distance similarity to original (incl. hidden) examples; Error = CM/SS (Eq. 3), fraction of synthetic samples closer to majority. Recommends ensembles (EasyEnsemble, Random Data Partitioning) over oversampling and real-world measurement of wrong predictions.
primary_metric: Error rate (fraction of synthetic samples closer to majority, Eq. 3)
protocol: Hide random 10%, 25% or 50% of majority examples, oversample remaining data, return hidden subset, compare synthetic samples to all original examples with Hassanat distance; no classifier training
stat_test_details: No statistical tests; methods compared by average error rate and average rank over 3 datasets.
reporting_details: Table 1: survey of 72 methods (datasets, classes, classifiers, metrics). Table 3 (text calls it Table 2): NE, SE, ER per dataset with average ER and average rank at 10% hidden. Fig. 3: box plots of error rates at 10/25/50% hidden. Fig. 4: average rank vs average error. Fig. 5: 2-feature visualization of SMOTE synthetic vs hidden majority samples. Table 4: ER of 8 best methods on Vehicle3 at 25% hidden. Fig. 1: publication-count trend.
key_result: All 72 oversamplers generate synthetic minority samples that lie closer to (hidden) majority examples (average ER from about 0.00 for DSMOTE to 0.99 for AHC/SUNDO), and the best performers degrade on Vehicle3, so the authors argue oversampling should be avoided in critical real-world applications.
eval_strengths: Introduces a classifier-free validity check of synthetic samples and applies it uniformly to 72 methods with several hidden fractions and 5 repeats.
eval_weaknesses: Only 3 (plus 1) closely related datasets, no downstream classification or statistical test, unclear nearest-neighbour decision rule, implementation and parameter settings of the 72 methods not stated, and the error measure assumes hidden majority neighbours imply wrong labels.
where: Sec. 2 Table 1 (review), Sec. 3 Eq. 1-3 and Fig. 2 (validation system), Sec. 4 Table 2, Sec. 5 Tables 3-4 and Figs. 3-5

title: Asymptotic Properties of Nearest Neighbor Rules Using Edited Data

datasets.notes: Four 1D two-class problems with known densities: logistic centered at -1 vs +1 (Fig. 1), N(0,1) vs N(1,1) (Fig. 2), N(0,1) vs N(0,4) (Fig. 3), N(-2,1) vs N(2,1) (Fig. 4). Proofs are stated for M classes but analysis uses M=2. No imbalance considered.

metric_details: Evaluation is theoretical: asymptotic (N to infinity) risk under 0-1 loss, i.e., error probability, of the K-NN rule and of the modified rule (edit each sample by K-NN of the others, delete if misclassified, then classify with 1-NN on the edited set) compared with the Bayes risk. Risk is computed analytically for the four problems as a function of K (1 to 20, Figs. 1-4), and local risk is plotted against the posterior p1(x) for K = 1,2 / 3,4 / 5,6 / 9,10 / 19,20 / 49,50 (Figs. 5-10); maximum ratio of local risk to Bayes risk is discussed. Convergence proved in probability (Theorems 1-4, Appendices I-III).
primary_metric: Error rate (asymptotic risk relative to Bayes risk)
protocol: Analytical asymptotic risk computation (no sampling, no train/test split)
tuning: Editing neighbourhood K varied analytically (1 to 50); 3-NN editing followed by 1-NN classification recommended; ties broken randomly.
reporting_details: Figs. 1-4: asymptotic risk vs K for K-NN and modified K-NN against Bayes risk on four distributions; Figs. 5-10: probability of deciding class 1 and local risk vs p1(x) for increasing K; Theorems 1-4 with proofs in Appendices I-III.
key_result: Editing with the 3-NN rule and then classifying with 1-NN on the edited set gives an asymptotic risk that approaches the Bayes risk closely, and the edited nearest neighbour converges in probability to the query point.
eval_strengths: Rigorous convergence proofs and exact asymptotic risk curves against the Bayes optimum on several distribution families.
eval_weaknesses: Purely asymptotic analysis on 1D balanced toy distributions; no finite-sample experiments, real data or imbalance-aware metrics (its use as an undersampling cleaner came later).
where: Sec. I (rule definitions, Figs. 1-4), Sec. III (asymptotic properties, Figs. 5-10), Sec. IV, Appendices I-III
flags: Drive text is partly scrambled OCR; exact numeric maximum risk ratios (around 1.07 to 1.2) not reliably legible, so omitted.

title: A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting

datasets.n_classes_range: 2 and k (theory covers binary, multiclass and regression)
datasets.notes: No experiments or datasets; purely theoretical. Initial weight distribution D over training examples is ordinarily uniform (D(i)=1/N), the hook later exploited by cost-sensitive boosting for imbalance.

metric_details: Theoretical guarantees only. Binary AdaBoost: training error of final hypothesis bounded by 2^T prod sqrt(eps_t(1-eps_t)) (Theorem 6), improved by factor two with soft threshold (Sec. 4.5). Generalization error bounded via VC-dimension of the combined class, at most 2(d+1)(T+1)log2(e(T+1)) (Theorems 7-8). AdaBoost.M1 uses multiclass prediction error (needs eps_t < 1/2); AdaBoost.M2 uses pseudo-loss with label weighting (Theorems 10-11); AdaBoost.R uses mean squared error. Hedge evaluated by net cumulative loss vs best strategy, O(sqrt(T ln N)).
primary_metric: Error rate (training and generalization error bounds)
protocol: Theoretical analysis (worst-case bounds); for choosing T suggests structural risk minimization or a held-out validation set ('cross-validation') in Sec. 4.3
tuning: Number of rounds T to be chosen by SRM bound or validation-set error; beta_t set adaptively from eps_t (no prior knowledge of weak-learner edge).
reporting_details: Algorithms in Figs. 1-5 (Hedge, AdaBoost, AdaBoost.M1, AdaBoost.M2, AdaBoost.R); Theorems 1-11 with proofs. Empirical claims (AdaBoost tends not to overfit; pseudo-loss helps with very restricted weak learners) are cited from other work [8, 12], not shown.
key_result: AdaBoost boosts any weak learner without knowing its edge, with training error decreasing exponentially in T and generalization controlled by the VC-dimension of the weighted vote; extensions handle multiclass (M1, M2) and regression (R).
eval_strengths: Rigorous, distribution-free error bounds for binary, multiclass and regression settings.
eval_weaknesses: No empirical evaluation at all in this paper; error rate is the only notion of performance and class imbalance is not considered.
where: Sec. 4 (4.1 Fig. 2, 4.2 Theorem 6, 4.3 Theorems 7-8), Sec. 5 (5.1-5.3, Figs. 3-5, Theorems 9-11)

sources: private (oil-spill radar images, sleep EEG data from TU Graz)

protocol: Stratified k-fold CV with k = 4 to 8 depending on domain (Table 3), results averaged over folds
tuning: No tuning reported; OSS is parameter-free (CNN-like consistent subset seeded with all positives plus one random negative, single 1-NN pass, then removal of negatives in Tomek links); classifier settings not stated.

title: SMOTE-IPF: Addressing the noisy and borderline examples problem in imbalanced classification by a re-sampling method with filtering

sources: synthetic generator of Napierala et al. [40,46]
datasets.notes: 30 synthetic 2-D sets (sub-cluster, clover, paw shapes; 600 ex IR=5 or 800 ex IR=7; disturbance ratio 0/30/50/60/70% borderline). 9 real sets chosen for many noisy/borderline minority examples; multiclass sets binarized by joining classes. protocol: 5 runs of stratified 5-fold cross-validation, results averaged (5 folds chosen to keep enough minority examples in test partitions)

title: Random Balance: Ensembles of variable priors classifiers for imbalanced data

datasets.notes: 20 HDDT sets (IR 2.33-42.00) and 66 KEEL binary sets (IR 1.82-129.44) derived from 16 original sets, many originally multiclass. Synthetic: 2-D two-Gaussian simulation (450 vs 50 points) used only for the illustrative diversity study (Sec. 5).

metric_details: AUC, F-measure (2PR/(P+R)) and G-mean sqrt(TPR*TNR) defined in Sec. 2; accuracy reported for completeness. ROC threshold varies the ensemble class-membership probability (J48 leaf probabilities with Laplace smoothing). A combined average rank (mean of per-metric average ranks over AUC, F-measure, G-mean, accuracy) is also given. Simulation uses ensemble error, individual error, AUC and pairwise kappa (diversity) in kappa-error diagrams.
protocol: Stratified 5x2-fold cross-validation (results averaged over 10 train/test runs); simulation: 200 iterations with freshly sampled train and test data
tuning: Ensemble size 100 (50 in base-classifier study because of SVM cost). SMOTE k=5, amounts 100/200/500% or until balance. Optimized variants (EopS/EopU/EopB, BAGopS/U/B) pick SMOTE and/or RUS amount from 10 levels (100 combos) by 5-fold internal CV on the training set maximizing AUC of a single tree. RbB threshold chosen in 0.0-1.0 step 0.05 maximizing accuracy + G-mean on validation data. MultiBoost 10 subcommittees. Random Balance itself needs no class-ratio tuning.
stat_test_details: Average ranks within three families (data-preprocessing-only, Bagging, Boosting) per metric; Friedman with Iman-Davenport correction, then Hochberg post-hoc vs the proposed method (alpha=0.05). No test on the combined rank (values not independent). Cross-family comparison of family winners with Iman-Davenport (Table 13). Simulation: two-tailed paired t-test (p < 0.005).
reporting_details: Table 7: per-dataset AUC, F-measure and G-mean of the three proposed methods only; Tables 8-13: average ranks with Hochberg p for AUC, F-measure, G-mean, accuracy, combined, and best-per-family; Fig. 7 AUC-rank vs F-rank scatter; Tables 14-15 fusion rules (average, product, majority vote); Tables 16-18 base classifiers; Fig. 8 performance vs ensemble size 5-100; Fig. 9 % datasets won vs size for method pairs; Figs. 3-5 ROC-space clouds, decision boundaries and kappa-error diagrams. Supplement: per-dataset AUC, F-measure, G-mean and accuracy for all methods of the Data-processing family (Tables 1-4) and Boosting family (Tables 9-12), plus per-dataset AUC and F-measure for fusion rules (Tables 13-16) and base classifiers (Tables 17-22).
key_result: Random Balance ensembles obtain the best AUC average rank in all three families with significant Hochberg differences except RB-Boost vs RUSBoost, and the best combined rank, while F-measure and G-mean advantages are weaker.
eval_strengths: Very large benchmark (86 datasets, 30 competitors including tuned variants), four metrics, family-wise Friedman/Iman-Davenport with Hochberg post-hoc, plus studies of fusion rule, base learner and ensemble size.
eval_weaknesses: Main per-dataset results only in supplement, family-wise testing (no single global comparison), no runtime, and tuned baselines optimize AUC for a single tree rather than the ensemble.

title: A systematic study of the class imbalance problem in convolutional neural networks

datasets.notes: Balanced benchmarks artificially imbalanced by subsampling the training set under two parametrized forms: step imbalance (rho = max/min class size, mu = fraction of minority classes 0.1-0.9) and linear imbalance (rho only). MNIST: 4050 step + 450 linear training sets; CIFAR-10: rho in {2,10,20,50}, mu in {0.2,0.5,0.8}, fixed lowest-label classes as minority; ImageNet: 3 step settings (mu=0.1/rho=10, 0.8/50, 0.9/100), 5 subsets. Test sets kept balanced (1000/class MNIST and CIFAR-10, 50/class ImageNet).

metric_details: Main metric: multi-class ROC AUC (Provost and Domingos), the average of per-class one-vs-rest AUCs, using scikit-learn (all thresholds from test responses, trapezoid rule); threshold-independent. Overall accuracy reported separately (Sec. 4.4, Fig. 6) mainly to show the effect of thresholding (dividing softmax outputs by estimated class priors). Accuracy explicitly argued to be misleading under imbalance (Sec. 3.4). Confusion matrices only in Appendix C.
protocol: Provided train/test split of each benchmark; training set artificially imbalanced, test set left balanced and unchanged; CIFAR-10 step imbalance additionally rerun 3 times on reshuffled stratified train/test splits (Appendix A)
n_runs: MNIST: 50 repetitions per parameter combination (random minority classes); CIFAR-10: 8 runs per case (4 base learning rates x 2 repeats), best kept; ImageNet: 1 run, 3 runs for highest imbalance
tuning: Architectures and training hyperparameters fixed from literature (SGD with momentum, fixed iterations per dataset so number of weight updates is constant across imbalance levels; no pretraining). CIFAR-10: base learning rate chosen from {0.05, 0.005, 0.0005, 0.00005} and the model with the best TEST-set score over all 8 runs was kept. Two-phase training: same hyperparameters with base LR x 0.1 in phase 2. Sampling always to full balance except Sec. 4.5 (partial ratios on MNIST rho=1000).
stat_test_details: No statistical tests; variability only discussed qualitatively (ImageNet runs differ by more than 4 AUC points, so 1-2 point differences may be noise).
reporting_details: Figs. 3-4: multi-class ROC AUC vs rho and vs number of minority classes (step imbalance) on MNIST and CIFAR-10; Fig. 5: linear imbalance; Table 4: ImageNet AUC per setting and run; Fig. 6: accuracy with and without thresholding; Fig. 7: partial over/undersampling ratios; Fig. 8: train/test accuracy convergence (overfitting check). Supplements (not read, described from titles): Appendix A reshuffled-split reruns for CIFAR-10, Appendix B additional convergence plots, Appendix C and C.2 confusion matrices (C.2 for CIFAR-10). Training cost noted (5 days per ResNet-10 on a GTX 1070) but no runtime comparison.
key_result: Imbalance strongly hurts CNNs (more so for complex tasks); random oversampling to full balance is best in almost all settings and does not overfit, while thresholding on priors is needed to maximize accuracy.
eval_strengths: Controlled, parametrized imbalance (step vs linear, rho and mu) with thousands of trained networks on MNIST, threshold-free multi-class AUC on a balanced fixed test set, and explicit separation of data-size and imbalance effects.
eval_weaknesses: Only random resampling (no SMOTE-type or loss-based methods), CIFAR-10 model selection on the test set (optimistic bias), very few ImageNet runs, no statistical tests, single architecture per dataset.
where: Sec. 3 (setup, 3.4 metrics), Sec. 4, Figs. 3-8, Table 4, Appendices A-C
flags: Supplements not read (large figure dumps per instructions). Study name used as method; approach set to oversampling since ROS is the recommended method.
cite_note: No separate arXiv version appeared in the top search results. Re-verified by batch filter=openalex call on 2026-10-18: count unchanged.

title: Modeling Tabular Data using Conditional GAN

datasets.n_classes_range: binary and multiclass labels (class counts not stated); 1 regression task
datasets.notes: Real: adult, census, covertype, credit (Kaggle credit card fraud), intrusion (KDD Cup 99), news (regression), MNIST12 and MNIST28 (binarized MNIST as 144/784 binary columns). Simulated oracles: Gaussian mixtures grid, gridr, ring and Bayesian networks asia, alarm, child, insurance (10k train/10k test each). Imbalance addressed is in categorical columns (636/1048 have a category above 90%), not the label; label IR not reported. Supp. Table 1 gives train/test sizes and column types.

metric_details: Simulated data: likelihood fitness Lsyn (likelihood of synthetic rows under the true oracle) and Ltest (likelihood of real test rows under an oracle refit on synthetic data, detects mode collapse). Real data: machine learning efficacy, i.e., train prediction models on synthetic data and test on the real test set (train-synthetic-test-real); F1 for binary tasks (adult, census, credit), macro-F1 for covertype and intrusion, accuracy for MNIST12/28, R2 for news; score averaged over several prediction models per dataset. Threshold and positive class not stated. Supp. Table 2 also lists accuracy, F1, macro-F1, micro-F1 of models trained on real data.
primary_metric: F1 (machine learning efficacy on real data)
protocol: Fixed train/test split per real dataset (e.g., adult 23k/10k, credit 264k/20k; Supp. Table 1); simulated train and test sets sampled independently from the oracle (10k/10k); generators fit on train only, evaluators trained on synthetic data and tested on real test data
tuning: All generators trained with batch size 500 for 300 epochs. CTGAN: WGAN-GP + PacGAN (pac 10), Adam lr 2e-4; TVAE: Adam lr 1e-3. Evaluation models chosen per dataset to give reasonable performance on real data with fixed settings (AdaBoost 50 estimators, DT depth 20/30, MLP 50/100 units; Supp. Table 2). Baseline generator hyperparameters not stated in the paper (deferred to the SDGym benchmark).
stat_test_details: No statistical tests; no variance or repeated runs reported.
reporting_details: Table 1: number of real datasets (of 8) on which each GAN beats CLBN and PrivBN (CTGAN 7 and 8); Table 2: averages per experiment group (GM sim., BN sim., real clf F1, real reg R2); Table 3: ablation (GMM5/GMM10/MinMax normalization, without training-by-sampling, without conditional vector, GAN loss variants) as relative change on real classification sets. Supplement: dataset statistics and URLs (Table 1), evaluator models and their real-data accuracy/F1/macro-F1/micro-F1/R2 (Table 2), full per-dataset Lsyn/Ltest and F1/macro-F1/accuracy/R2 results with an aggregated rank per method in brackets (Table 3, method labels contain typos such as TVAE(3) and TGAN), and CTGAN training pseudo-code (Algorithm 1).
key_result: CTGAN beats both Bayesian network baselines on most real datasets in machine learning efficacy (7/8 vs CLBN, 8/8 vs PrivBN) while prior GANs do not, and its conditional generator with training-by-sampling is critical on imbalanced data (credit F1 drops to 0 without it).
eval_strengths: Open benchmark mixing simulated oracles (allowing likelihood-based fidelity) with real datasets, multiple evaluators averaged, Identity upper bound and a component ablation.
eval_weaknesses: Not evaluated as a minority oversampler for imbalanced classification (synthetic data replaces rather than augments training data), single split with no repeats, variance or statistical tests, label imbalance not quantified, F1 positive class and threshold unspecified.
where: Sec. 5 (5.1 datasets, 5.2 metrics, 5.3 results, 5.4 ablation), Fig. 3, Tables 1-3; Supplement Tables 1-3

title: A hybrid data-level ensemble to enable learning from highly imbalanced dataset

datasets.notes: 28 KEEL datasets (KEEL max IR about 100) plus 14 LibSVM datasets made highly imbalanced by randomly removing minority instances (all IR > 9, 4 with IR > 400); a pre-experiment confirmed class-wise accuracy differences on the 14. 129 to 20,034 instances, 3 to 5,000 features (Table 1). Datasets uploaded to GitHub. 13 datasets with IR > 50 analysed separately. Group-2 comparison tables (7-9) include a few KEEL sets not listed in Table 1 (e.g., Glass6, Glass4, Yeast2vs8). Experiment 2 drops cod, gisette and skinnonskin for cost.

metric_details: AUC and G-mean chosen as standard for imbalance; accuracy explicitly rejected. How AUC is obtained from C4.5 ensemble outputs and the G-mean definition/threshold are not stated. Group-2 comparison uses AUC only.
protocol: 5-fold stratified CV repeated 10 times (5x10 CV); group-2 baselines (CBIS, SNGEIP, sNED) compared using results copied from their original papers
tuning: All ensembles use 40 C4.5 base classifiers. Group-1 baselines run from KEEL implementations (their parameter values not stated). HD-Ensemble defaults k=5, lambda=0.85, q=30, justified by Experiment 2 sensitivity runs on the same benchmark datasets (lambda 0.5-1.0 step 0.05 with q=30; q 10-100 step 10); no per-dataset tuning.
stat_test_details: Friedman over 8 ensembles on 42 datasets (p=0.00 for AUC and G-mean), then Holm post-hoc with HD-Ensemble as control at alpha=0.05 (all 7 hypotheses rejected, Tables 5-6). Wilcoxon signed-rank vs each group-2 method on AUC (Table 10, p=0.0017, 0.0105, 0).
reporting_details: Table 3/4: mean +/- std AUC and G-mean per dataset for 8 ensembles (best bold, worst underlined) with average row and Best/Worst counts (G-mean: HD 28/1, IIVotes 1/30); Figs. 5-6: scatter of HD-Ensemble vs each competitor per dataset against the y=x line; Figs. 7-8: Friedman average rankings; Tables 5-6: Holm z, p and adjusted alpha; Tables 7-9: per-dataset AUC vs CBIS, SNGEIP, sNED with IR; Table 10: Wilcoxon R+/R-/p; Figs. 9-10: average rankings vs lambda and q (also serving as an ablation of under- vs oversampling share).
key_result: HD-Ensemble gives the best AUC on 33/42 datasets (average 0.9144 vs 0.8753 for SMOTEBoost) and best G-mean on 28/42 (0.8124 vs 0.7973 for UnderBagging), significantly better than all 10 competing ensembles per Friedman-Holm and Wilcoxon tests.
eval_strengths: Many highly imbalanced datasets up to IR 970, repeated stratified 5x10 CV, two complementary metrics, Friedman + Holm and Wilcoxon tests, equal ensemble size for all methods, and per-dataset tables with std.
eval_weaknesses: Single base learner, AUC/G-mean computation unspecified, default parameters chosen on the same benchmark datasets, group-2 comparison uses numbers copied from other papers (possibly different folds and protocols), 14 datasets artificially imbalanced by random minority removal, no runtime despite costly sequential training.

title: KNNOR: An oversampling technique for imbalanced datasets

sources: UTKFace and CIFAR-10 (qualitative image demo only)
datasets.notes: 19 small datasets randomly drawn from 62 KEEL-style sets with fewer than 1000 instances (Table 2: 177 to 900 instances); multiclass UCI sets binarized by grouping classes. Image experiments (UTKFace male vs female, CIFAR-10 airplane vs rest) only show generated images, no metrics. A simulated two-cluster set (Fig. 14) and IRIS/Haberman/thyroid plots are illustrations only.

metric_details: G-score = sqrt(TPR x TNR); F1 on the minority (positive) class; AUC as area under ROC; P20 = share of true positives among the top 20% of test points ranked by positive-class probability (20% used instead of 20 points because some sets have fewer than 20 positives). Threshold for F1/G not stated. Metrics follow Kovacs' smote-variants benchmark.
protocol: Repeated stratified 5-fold CV with 3 repeats, identical folds for all oversamplers (following Kovacs' smote-variants evaluation)
tuning: Up to 35 randomly chosen parameter combinations per oversampler and 6 per classifier (SVM C in {1,10} with L1/L2 and hinge/squared hinge; kNN k in {3,5,7}, uniform/distance; DT gini/entropy, max depth 3/5/unbounded; MLP 1 hidden layer, ReLU/logistic, 10/50/100% of features as units); for each dataset, oversampler and classifier the top result over these combinations is kept (3996 results, over 2 million jobs). No separate validation split mentioned.
stat_test_details: No statistical tests; comparison based on mean scores over datasets and average ranks.
reporting_details: Table 5: top 9 oversamplers per metric (AUC, F1, G, P20) and classifier by mean score over 19 datasets, with SMOTE and no-oversampling baselines; Table 6: overall ranking by averaging metrics over classifiers and taking the mean of per-metric ranks (KNNOR rank 1 on all four); Fig. 22: frequency of each rank per oversampler; Figs. 19-21: synthetic points from KNNOR and other oversamplers on Haberman/thyroid with varying k and distance threshold; Figs. 23-24: generated face and airplane images. Per-dataset results said to be in additional documents (not in this batch).
key_result: Averaged over 19 KEEL datasets and four classifiers, KNNOR obtains the best mean rank on AUC, F1, G-mean and P20 against Kovacs' top-10 oversamplers, SMOTE and no oversampling, and ranks first more often than any competitor.
eval_strengths: Strong, well-chosen baseline set (top 10 from an 85-method benchmark) evaluated in a common framework with four classifiers, four imbalance-aware metrics and identical repeated stratified folds.
eval_weaknesses: Best-of-grid results selected on the CV test folds (optimistic), only 19 small low-to-moderate IR datasets, no statistical tests, per-dataset results not in the paper, image experiment purely qualitative, no runtime despite a large parameter search.
flags: Table 6 column labels look swapped (values under 'G' match F1 scale, under 'F1' match P20, under 'P20' match G) and row order is not sorted by average rank (CCR 7.5 listed 2nd). Abstract speaks of 'accuracy of classifiers' but the reported metrics are AUC, F1, G and P20. resampling_inside_cv not stated (framework from Kovacs likely oversamples training folds only).
